title: Keep the rows you want

outcomes.can: Combine tests and control which one is applied first.
Tell a text value from a column name.
Match a pattern and an inclusive range.

intro: Most questions are about some of the rows, not all of them. WHERE keeps the rows that pass a test. This module covers comparisons, combining tests with AND and OR, and matching lists, ranges and patterns.

steps.title: Keep the rows that pass a test
steps.text: WHERE comes after FROM and holds a condition. A row is kept only when the condition is true for it. The comparison operators are = (equal), <> (not equal), <, <=, > and >=. Text values go in single quotes: country = 'USA'. Double quotes mean something else in SQL. They mark a name, such as a column, so "USA" would be read as a column called USA.

steps.title: Count the rows kept
steps.text: Department 3 is Sales. Predict how many rows come back.

steps.title: Follow the filter
steps.text: The employees table has 24 rows. The condition department_id = 3 is tested on each one, and four pass: Priya, Hannah, Ravi and Julia. The SELECT list then decides which of their columns are shown. A column used in WHERE does not have to be in the SELECT list.

steps.title: Combine tests
steps.text: AND keeps a row only when both sides are true. OR keeps it when at least one side is true. NOT flips a test. When a condition mixes them, AND is applied before OR, the way multiplication comes before addition. Use brackets to say what you mean. Three shorter forms are common. department_id IN (4, 5) is true when the value is any one in the list. price BETWEEN 50 AND 100 includes both ends. LIKE matches text against a pattern, where % stands for any run of characters, including none: last_name LIKE 'S%' matches names that start with S, and title LIKE '%Engineer%' matches titles that contain Engineer.

steps.title: Which test is applied first?
steps.text: The condition mixes OR and AND with no brackets. Predict which Marketing employees (department 4) appear.

steps.title: Follow AND before OR
steps.text: AND binds first, so the condition reads as: department 5, or (department 4 and salary above 90000). Everyone in department 5 is kept whatever they earn. From department 4, only Tom and Laura pass the salary test. Kofi, on 88000, is left out. With brackets around the OR, the salary test would apply to both departments.

steps.title: Double quotes around text
steps.text: The city is written in double quotes. Read the example before checking.

steps.title: Read the error
steps.text: Check the example. Error 42703 says column "Denver" does not exist. Double quotes mark a name, so PostgreSQL looked for a column called Denver. Write the text value in single quotes: city = 'Denver'.

steps.title: List what can be sold
steps.text: The starter filters on stock only. Add the second test.

steps.title: Find small, cheap items
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Think about which test must be applied first.

choices.feedback: WHERE keeps only the rows whose department_id is 3.
The test is applied to every row, and every row that passes is kept.
AND is applied first, so the salary test belongs to department 4 only, and Kofi earns less than 90000.
The salary test applies to department 4, and Kofi's 88000 does not pass it.
The row is kept when either side of the OR is true, and two Marketing employees pass the right side.

questions.prompt: What happens when you check this example?

choices.text: It returns the customers who live in Denver.
choices.feedback: Double quotes do not make a text value. They make a name.
The statement does not run at all. It has an error.

choices.text: PostgreSQL reports an error on line 3.
choices.feedback: "Denver" is read as a column name, and there is no such column (42703).

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.

drillGap: These drills practise one kind of test each. They do not mix AND with OR or test a value that sits on a limit.
